items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the lowest layer of the atmosphere, up to about 8-17 km, where temperature falls with height and weather occurs”?
items.answer: Troposphere
items.markingKey: Troposphere: the lowest layer of the atmosphere, up to about 8-17 km, where temperature falls with height and weather occurs. [1]

items.stem: Explain why temperature decreases with height in the troposphere.
items.answer: The atmosphere is heated mainly from below by the ground, which absorbs solar radiation and emits infrared; air further from the surface receives less heat, and rising air expands and cools as pressure falls.
items.markingKey: heated from the ground [1]; expansion / lower pressure [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how the composition of the atmosphere has changed since 1750.
items.answer: Carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 to over 420 ppm; methane has more than doubled; nitrous oxide has increased; new gases such as CFCs have been added; stratospheric ozone was depleted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per change, with data up to [3]

items.stem: At a town at the foot of Aconcagua (500 m above sea level) the air temperature is 18 °C. The summit is 6 961 m above sea level. Assume an environmental lapse rate of 6.5 °C per 1000 m. Calculate the expected temperature at the summit.

At a town at the foot of Mount Kinabalu (1 000 m above sea level) the air temperature is 17 °C. The summit is 4 095 m above sea level. Assume an environmental lapse rate of 6.5 °C per 1000 m. (a) Explain why air temperature falls with height in the troposphere. (b) Suggest why the actual temperature at the summit may differ from your calculation.
items.answer: (a) The troposphere is heated from the ground; air pressure falls with height, so air expands and cools. (b) The lapse rate varies with humidity, time of day, cloud and weather; temperature inversions may occur; wind and aspect affect local temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) heated from below [1]; expansion with lower pressure [1] [2] (b) 1 mark per reason up to [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the composition of the atmosphere is now controlled more by human activities than by natural processes. In your answer you should consider: carbon cycle; trace gases.
items.answer: For: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation have raised CO₂ by about 50%; methane from agriculture has more than doubled; CFCs damaged the ozone layer. Against: Nitrogen, oxygen and argon (over 99% of dry air) are controlled by natural cycles; volcanic eruptions and photosynthesis still dominate many fluxes. Judgement: Natural processes still control the bulk composition, but human activity now controls the trace gases that matter most for climate and ozone.

items.stem: A student writes: “The atmosphere gets thinner with height.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Air pressure and density fall with altitude because gravity holds most of the air near the surface.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the circulation cell between the equator and about 30° latitude, with rising air at the equator and sinking air in the subtropics”?
items.answer: Hadley cell
items.markingKey: Hadley cell: the circulation cell between the equator and about 30° latitude, with rising air at the equator and sinking air in the subtropics. [1]

items.stem: Explain the formation of the Hadley cell.
items.answer: Intense heating at the equator causes air to rise (low pressure, ITCZ); it cools and moves polewards at high altitude; it sinks at about 30°, forming high pressure; surface trade winds return air to the equator.
items.markingKey: rising at equator [1]; poleward flow aloft [1]; sinking at 30° [1]; trade winds return [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why the tropical rainforest has high rainfall throughout the year.
items.answer: Strong heating causes convection; air rises at the ITCZ, cools, water vapour condenses and heavy convectional rain falls most afternoons; the ITCZ stays close to the equator.
items.markingKey: heating / rising air [1]; condensation [1]; ITCZ position [1] [3]

items.stem: A student in Mexico City is comparing climate graphs for Manaus (3° S, tropical rainforest), Kano (12° N, savanna) and Riyadh (25° N, hot desert). Explain why Manaus has high rainfall all year.
items.answer: It lies near the ITCZ all year; intense heating causes rising air, condensation and convectional rain.

items.stem: Fig. 3.2 shows the tricellular model of atmospheric circulation, with the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells and the main pressure belts and surface winds. (a) Describe the pattern of pressure at the surface from the equator to 30° N. (b) Suggest one limitation of the tricellular model.
items.answer: (a) Low pressure at the equator (ITCZ), rising to high pressure at about 30° N (subtropical high). (b) It ignores the effects of land and sea, mountains, seasonal shifts and monsoons.

items.stem: A student in Karachi is comparing climate graphs for Manaus (3° S, tropical rainforest), Kano (12° N, savanna) and Riyadh (25° N, hot desert). (a) Describe the pattern of pressure at the surface from the equator to 30° N. (b) Explain why Manaus has high rainfall all year.
items.answer: (a) Low pressure at the equator (ITCZ), rising to high pressure at about 30° N (subtropical high). (b) It lies near the ITCZ all year; intense heating causes rising air, condensation and convectional rain.

items.stem: Explain how the movement of the ITCZ causes wet and dry seasons in the savanna.
items.answer: The ITCZ follows the overhead Sun; when it moves over the savanna, rising air brings rain (wet season); when it moves away, subtropical high pressure brings sinking, dry air (dry season).
items.markingKey: ITCZ follows overhead sun [1]; rain when overhead [1]; high pressure / dry when away [1] [3]

items.stem: Fig. 3.2 shows the tricellular model of atmospheric circulation, with the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells and the main pressure belts and surface winds. (a) Explain why Riyadh receives very little rain. (b) Explain the seasonal pattern of rainfall in Kano.
items.answer: (a) It lies under the descending limb of the Hadley cell; sinking air warms and is dry, giving high pressure and clear skies. (b) Rain falls in summer when the ITCZ moves north over the area; in winter the ITCZ moves south and dry north-east trade winds (the Harmattan) bring a dry season.

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the natural warming of the Earth as greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation from the surface”?
items.answer: Greenhouse effect
items.markingKey: Greenhouse effect: the natural warming of the Earth as greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared radiation from the surface. [1]

items.stem: Explain how the greenhouse effect warms the Earth.
items.answer: Short-wave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere and heats the surface; the surface emits long-wave infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb it and re-emit some back towards the surface, keeping the lower atmosphere warmer.
items.markingKey: short-wave in [1]; long-wave out [1]; absorption and re-emission [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain two positive feedback mechanisms that could accelerate global warming.
items.answer: Melting ice and snow expose darker surfaces with lower albedo, absorbing more heat; thawing permafrost releases methane and CO₂; warmer air holds more water vapour, a greenhouse gas; warmer oceans absorb less CO₂.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per mechanism, 1 mark per explanation [4]

items.stem: Name one example of a country vulnerable to climate change you have studied and, for that example, describe the impacts of climate change on the country.
items.answer: Bangladesh: Much of the country is less than 10 m above sea level; sea level rise and stronger cyclones increase storm surges; saltwater intrusion damages rice fields and drinking water; more intense monsoon floods; millions may be displaced by 2050.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. sea level, storms, flooding, agriculture, water, with data [4]

items.stem: Explain how CFCs cause ozone depletion.
items.answer: CFCs drift into the stratosphere where UV breaks them down, releasing chlorine atoms; chlorine reacts with ozone (Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂) and is regenerated, so a single atom destroys many ozone molecules.
items.markingKey: UV breaks CFC [1]; chlorine released [1]; catalytic chain reaction [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why ozone depletion is greatest over Antarctica.
items.answer: Very cold winter temperatures form polar stratospheric clouds; reactions on their surfaces convert chlorine into reactive forms; when sunlight returns in spring, rapid ozone destruction occurs; the polar vortex isolates the air.
items.markingKey: cold / clouds [1]; chlorine activated [1]; spring sunlight / vortex [1] [3]

“The Montreal Protocol shows that international agreements can solve global environmental problems.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Ratified by all 198 UN members; ozone-depleting substance production fell by about 99%; the ozone layer is recovering; it also avoided warming because CFCs are greenhouse gases. Against: Ozone depletion was easier to solve than climate change: few producers, cheap substitutes and clear evidence; illegal CFC-11 emissions from China were detected in 2018; recovery will take decades. Judgement: It shows that agreements can succeed when science is clear and alternatives exist, but its success may be hard to repeat for more complex problems.

items.stem: Explain how acid rain damages forests and lakes.
items.answer: Acid rain leaches nutrients such as calcium and magnesium from soils and releases toxic aluminium, damaging roots and weakening trees; in lakes low pH and aluminium damage fish gills and kill eggs and invertebrates.

items.stem: Explain why acid rain is a transboundary problem.

Evaluate the view that the tricellular model explains the distribution of the world’s climates.
items.answer: For: It explains the wet equatorial belt (ITCZ), subtropical deserts at 30°, wet mid-latitudes with westerly winds and polar highs. Actions that reduce greenhouse gas emissions or remove them from the atmosphere to limit climate change.

items.stem: Assess the extent to which adaptation is now more important than mitigation in responding to climate change. Support your answer with examples. In your answer you should consider: vulnerable countries; costs.
items.answer: For: Some warming is already locked in, so sea walls, drought-resistant crops and early warning systems (Bangladesh) are urgently needed to protect people now. Against: Without mitigation (renewables, efficiency, forest protection) warming could exceed 3 °C and overwhelm adaptation; mitigation addresses the cause and is cheaper in the long term. Judgement: Both are essential: mitigation limits future damage while adaptation manages unavoidable impacts, especially in vulnerable countries.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “enhanced greenhouse effect”?
options: The extra warming caused by increased concentrations of greenhouse gases from human activities.
A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a period (usually 100 years) compared with the same mass of carbon dioxide.
Actions that reduce greenhouse gas emissions or remove them from the atmosphere to limit climate change.
Actions that reduce the harmful effects of climate change, such as sea walls or drought-resistant crops.
items.answer: The extra warming caused by increased concentrations of greenhouse gases from human activities.
items.markingKey: Enhanced greenhouse effect: the extra warming caused by increased concentrations of greenhouse gases from human activities. [1]

items.stem: Describe the evidence that the climate is changing.
items.answer: Rising global temperatures in instrumental records; shrinking glaciers and Arctic sea ice; rising sea level; ice cores showing CO₂ and temperature; changes in species ranges and earlier spring events.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per piece of evidence up to [3]

items.stem: Table 3.3 shows annual carbon dioxide emissions (million tonnes) and population (millions) for selected countries (2022 estimates): Qatar 100 Mt, 2.7 million; Germany 670 Mt, 84 million; Brazil 480 Mt, 215 million. Calculate the emissions per person (tonnes) for each country.
items.answer: Qatar 37.0 t; Germany 7.98 t; Brazil 2.23 t
items.markingKey: emissions ÷ population [1]; all correct [1] [2]

items.stem: Name one example of a country vulnerable to climate change you have studied and, for that example, evaluate the strategies used to respond to climate change.
items.answer: Bangladesh: Over 4000 cyclone shelters and an early warning system have cut cyclone deaths dramatically; floating gardens and salt-tolerant rice; embankments; the Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. adaptation (and mitigation) measures; success and limits; judgement [4]

items.stem: Elena argues that the impacts of climate change will be greater for low-income countries than for high-income countries. Discuss this view, referring to named examples.
items.answer: For: Low-income countries depend on rain-fed farming, have less money for defences and are often in hot or low-lying regions (the Sahel, Bangladesh). Against: High-income countries also face severe heatwaves, wildfires and floods (Europe 2021, Australia 2019-20); some high-latitude areas may benefit from longer growing seasons. Judgement: Impacts are global, but vulnerability and capacity to adapt make them most severe for low-income countries.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using named examples and data, with a reasoned judgement. Level 2 (3-5 marks): developed points but limited balance or exemplification. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple, generalised points. [8]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “CFC replacements such as HFCs are harmless to the environment.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. HFCs do not deplete ozone but are powerful greenhouse gases, so the Kigali Amendment phases them down.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe the impacts of ozone depletion on ecosystems.
items.answer: More UV-B damages phytoplankton, reducing productivity at the base of marine food chains; damages DNA in plants and animals; reduces crop yields; harms amphibian eggs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per impact up to [2]

items.stem: Mean minimum total ozone over Antarctica in October was about 310 Dobson units (DU) in the 1970s, fell to 140 DU in 2000 and was 140 DU in 2022. Values below 220 DU are classed as an ozone hole. Recovery is about 1 DU per year on average. Estimate the year in which ozone would return above 220 DU.
items.answer: about 2102

items.stem: “The Montreal Protocol shows that international agreements can solve global environmental problems.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to examples you have studied.
items.answer: For: Ratified by all 198 UN members; ozone-depleting substance production fell by about 99%; the ozone layer is recovering; it also avoided warming because CFCs are greenhouse gases. Against: Ozone depletion was easier to solve than climate change: few producers, cheap substitutes and clear evidence; illegal CFC-11 emissions from China were detected in 2018; recovery will take decades. Judgement: It shows that agreements can succeed when science is clear and alternatives exist, but its success may be hard to repeat for more complex problems.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 4 (16-20 marks): comprehensive, well-structured essay; detailed knowledge of named examples; sustained evaluation and a well-supported conclusion. Level 3 (11-15 marks): good knowledge and examples, some evaluation, conclusion partly supported. Level 2 (6-10 marks): relevant but mainly descriptive, limited examples or one-sided. Level 1 (1-5 marks): a few simple, generalised points with little or no evaluation. [20]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Photochemical smog is worst on cold, cloudy winter days.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It needs strong sunlight to drive the reactions, so it is worst on hot, sunny, still days.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Daily mean PM2.5 concentrations (μg/m³) recorded in Cairo during one week: Mon 76, Tue 22, Wed 97, Thu 95, Fri 42, Sat 87, Sun 89. The WHO 24-hour guideline is 15 μg/m³. Suggest reasons for the variation between days.
items.answer: Changes in weather (wind speed, rain, inversions); traffic differences between weekdays and weekends; episodes of burning or industrial activity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason up to [2]

items.stem: Daily mean PM2.5 concentrations (μg/m³) recorded in Cairo during one week: Mon 67, Tue 154, Wed 150, Thu 122, Fri 132, Sat 134, Sun 117. The WHO 24-hour guideline is 15 μg/m³. (a) Calculate the range of the daily values. (b) Explain why PM2.5 is particularly harmful to health.
items.answer: (a) 87 μg/m³ (b) The particles are so small that they penetrate deep into the alveoli and enter the bloodstream, causing respiratory and heart disease.
